TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       The intervenors, Newman Surface Properties, LP (NSP) and Cherokee Camp, LLC

(Cherokee Camp) (collectively the Newman Group), timely file this their Initial Brief in the above-

                                    Newman Group’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief


I.      INTRODUCTION

        1.       The Newman Group respectfully requests that the Public Utility Commission of

Texas (the Commission) select Route 894 as the route that best meets all applicable routing criteria

under the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) and the Commission’s substantive rules, and that

the Commission decline to select Route 295, Route 296, Route 572, or Cherokee Creek RFI Route

CCG (CCG), each of which are materially inferior to Route 894 for the reasons set forth below.

        2.       The Newman Group takes no position on whether the Bell County East Switch to

Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project (the Project) is necessary or serves the public

interest. The Newman Group intervened solely to address the routing question: if a certificate of

convenience and necessity is granted, which among the filed route alternatives best minimizes

impacts to landowners, communities, parks, and the environment while remaining cost-effective,

as PURA Section 37.056(c)(4) and the Commission’s rules require? On that question, the record

points in one direction.

        3.       Route 894 has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline.1 That figure

is near the minimum of all 122 filed routes, whose range extends from 80 structures on the least-

impactful routes to well over 100 on many others.2 By comparison, the routes the Newman Group

cannot support (Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG) have 104, 105, 107, and 105 habitable structures

– between 19 and 22 more than Route 894.3 Oncor’s routing expert, Brenda Perkins, confirmed

that Route 894’s primary strengths are length, cost, and habitable structures — and that length,

cost, and habitable structures are the factors the Commission has historically treated as most

2 See Oncor & LCRA – TSC Ex. 5, C. Petty Dir. Test. at 43.

3 See Oncor & LCRA – TSC Ex. 1A, Errata to Table 7-2 at 158,183, & 211. (Comparing Routes 295, 296, 572 to

894); see also Cherokee Creek Ptnrs. Ex. No. 20, Oncor & LCRA – TSC Resp. to CCP RFI 3-01, at 6.

important in route selection.4 This record finding alone provides a strong and independent basis

for selecting Route 894.

          4.       Beyond the objective structure counts, the Newman Group has direct and concrete

stakes in two specific links that distinguish Route 894 from the routes it cannot support. Link J6 –

used by Routes 295, 296, and CCG– bisects Cherokee Camp’s high-fenced commercial hunting

ranch diagonally from northwest to southeast, passing directly through Soldier’s Hole, a historically

significant site that is central to the ranch’s cultural and natural heritage.5 Link K41 – used by

Route 572 – passes within approximately 450 feet of an occupied dwelling on NSP’s Tract 1447,

placing that structure squarely within the Commission’s 500-foot prudent avoidance zone for high-

voltage transmission facilities.6 Route 894 uses neither Link J6 nor Link K41.7 For this reason,

among others, the Newman Group supports Route 894.

          5.       This brief is organized as follows. Section II summarizes the legal standard

governing the Commission’s route selection decision. Section III describes the Newman Group’s

properties and interests. Section IV demonstrates that Route 894 best meets all applicable routing

criteria. Section V explains why Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG each fail to meet those criteria

and must be rejected. Section VI presents the Newman Group’s conclusion and formal request for

relief.

II.       LEGAL STANDARD

          6.       Section 37.056(c)(4) of PURA provides that in determining whether to grant a CCN

for a transmission line, the Commission shall consider the effects of the line on the communities it


4 See Tr. Vol. 2 at 94:22 – 95:1.

5 See Newman Group Ex. No. 2, K. Newman Dir. Test. at 0024:18 – 23 & 0026:10 – 0027:2.

6 See Newman Group Ex. No. 1, K. Newman Dir. Test. at 0007:10 – 13.

7 See Oncor & LCRA – TSC Ex. No. 5, C. Petty Dir. Test. at 12:4 – 7.

                                        Newman Group’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief


serves, including: (A) community values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic

values, and the economic development of the state; (B) the use of the shortest or least cost route;

(C) the use of existing rights-of-way; and (D) the impact of the transmission line on the

environment.8 These criteria do not operate in isolation as confirmed by former PUC Chairman

Smitherman.9 The Commission must weigh them as a whole, giving appropriate effect to the

record evidence on each factor as applied to each alternate route.

         7.        Commission Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) implements PURA Section

37.056(c)(4) by specifying a nonexclusive list of routing factors that the Commission shall consider,

including the “prudent avoidance of residences” within 500 feet of the transmission line

centerline.10 The Newman Group argues prudent avoidance is not a minimum-compliance

standard that a route satisfies simply by not exceeding some threshold. Rather, the Newman Group

asserts it is an affirmative obligation to minimize residential proximity to the extent practicable

given all other routing considerations. A route that unnecessarily places a 765-kV transmission line

within 500 feet of 104, 105, or 107 habitable structures when a comparable route can achieve 85

cannot be said to have applied prudent avoidance; it simply tolerates avoidable harm.

         8.        The Commission exercises independent judgment in evaluating competing routing

alternatives. It is not bound by the Applicants’ designation of a “best-meets” route, nor by any

other party’s preferences.11 The Commission’s task is to determine, based on the full evidentiary

10 See 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

11 See, e.g., Application of Sharyland Utilities, L.P., PUC Dkt. No. 35236, Final Order, at ¶ 48 (stating that the Commission

exercises independent judgment in evaluating routing alternatives and is not bound by any party’s designation of a
“best-meets” route).

record, which route objectively best meets the full constellation of criteria that PURA and the

Commission’s rules specify. For the reasons set forth below, that route is Route 894.

III.         THE NEWMAN GROUP’S PROPERTIES AND INTERESTS

             9.     Cherokee Camp is a limited liability company that owns high-fenced ranch

property in San Saba County, Texas.12 The ranch is operated as a commercial paid-hunting

operation, and the Newman family has invested substantially in developing it for that purpose.13

Kevin Newman described the ranch’s physical layout, its wildlife management infrastructure, and

the specific location of Link J6’s proposed centerline relative to the ranch boundaries and

improvements.14 His testimony establishes that Link J6 would bisect the ranch diagonally from

northwest to southeast, running through the interior rather than along any boundary, and that the

bisection would sever the perimeter fence system and disrupt wildlife management operations

across the entirety of the affected corridor.15

             10.    The most significant concern for Cherokee Camp is Soldier’s Hole; a historically

significant site located on the ranch property within the Link J6 corridor.16 Soldier’s Hole carries

historical significance tied to the area’s frontier history.17 Although Soldier’s Hole does not bear a

Texas Historical Commission marker, its significance is documented in the record.18 The

Commission is required under PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(C) to give weight to “historical and

aesthetic values” in its route selection.19 The imposition of a 765-kV transmission corridor through

a historically significant site on private land – a site that can neither be relocated nor replicated –

is precisely the kind of irreversible harm that the statute directs the Commission to avoid where a

viable alternative exists. Route 894 provides that alternative.

          11.       NSP is a limited partnership that owns contiguous ranching tracts in San Saba

County and Mason County, Texas, including Tract 1447.20 NSP’s primary concern is Link K41.21

The Link K41 centerline passes within approximately 450 feet of an occupied dwelling on Tract

1447.22 That distance places the dwelling within the Commission’s 500-foot prudent avoidance

zone. Moreover, testimony at the hearing confirmed that the 500-foot threshold – already

established as a zone of concern for lower-voltage transmission facilities – does not fully account

for the impacts of a 765-kV facility, which may extend beyond the conventional 500-foot prudent-

avoidance metric.23 Routing a 765-kV line within 450 feet of a habitable structure when a viable

alternative is available is not consistent with prudent avoidance. Route 894 avoids Link K41

entirely and therefore avoids this impact altogether.

IV.       ROUTE 894 BEST MEETS ALL APPLICABLE ROUTING CRITERIA

          12.       Route 894 is comprised of the following link sequence: A0-A1-A2-B1-B21-C4-D12-

C5-E52-F1-F31-F32-F20-F23-G72-G73-G82-G13-G51-G52-H1-H41-H42-J21-J22-J23-J27-J4-

K11-K7-J16-K13-K51-K52-M11-M12-N3-P2-R1-T1-T2-Z2.24 Route 894 does not use Link J6

or Link K41, the two links most critical to the Newman Group’s landowner interests.25 As

demonstrated below, Route 894’s advantages over the routes the Newman Group cannot support

are not merely a matter of landowner preference; they are reflected in the objective routing metrics

that the Commission’s rules require the Commission to weigh.

             A.      Route 894 Minimizes Habitable Structure Impacts

             13.     Habitable structures within 500 feet of the transmission line centerline are one of

the major routing factors considered by the Commission. Staff witness Poole acknowledged on

cross-examination that habitable structures, cost, length, paralleling, and environmental integrity

are all “major factors” in route evaluation.26 On that measure, Route 894 outperforms Routes 295,

296, 572, and CCG. The record data is unambiguous. Route 894 has 85 habitable structures

within 500 feet of its centerline. Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG have 104, 105, 107, and 105

habitable structures.27 Stated differently, selecting Route 295 instead of Route 894 would expose

19 additional households to a 765-kV transmission line within the Commission’s own prudent

avoidance distance. Selecting Route 296 would expose 20 additional households. Selecting Route

572 would expose 22 additional households. Selecting CCG would expose 20 additional

households. None of these incremental burdens is justified by any offsetting advantage in the

record.

             14.     Among the 122 filed routes, the minimum habitable structure count is 80 (Routes

430 and 442).28 Route 894’s count of 85 places it among the very best-performing routes in the

proceeding on this criterion – within five structures of the minimum. The routes the Newman

26 See Tr. Vol. 4 at 197:14 – 17 (Poole Cross by S. Herrera).

27 See Supra FN 3.

28 See Oncor & LCRA – TSC Ex. No. 5 at 43: bullet pt. 3.

                                      Newman Group’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief


Group cannot support are 24 to 27 structures above the minimum. The Commission’s prudent

avoidance policy requires the Commission to select the route that minimizes residential proximity

to the extent practicable. On this major routing factor, Route 894 is the clear choice.

         B.       Route 894 Best Protects Community and Historical Values

         15.      PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(A - E) directs the Commission to consider community

values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and

the economic development of the state in evaluating competing routes.29 Route 894 excels on each

of these dimensions. It avoids the two links that would impose the most severe community and

historical impacts – Link J6 and Link K41 – and it achieves the best possible outcome on parks

proximity of any route in the proceeding.

                  1.       Route 894 Avoids Link J6 and Soldier’s Hole

         16.      Routes 295, 296, and CCG use Link J6.30 Link J6’s proposed centerline bisects

Cherokee Camp’s commercial hunting ranch diagonally from northwest to southeast, passing

directly through the interior of the high-perimeter fence and through the location of Soldier’s

Hole.31 The impacts of a 765-kV transmission corridor on a high-fenced commercial hunting

operation are not speculative: the corridor would require clearing a permanent right-of-way

through the interior of the ranch; the high perimeter fence that is essential to the ranch’s

commercial hunting model would be severed and rebuilt in sections, altering wildlife containment

patterns; feeding stations, blinds, and other hunting infrastructure within the corridor would be

displaced; and noise and electromagnetic effects from the transmission line would disrupt wildlife

behavior within and adjacent to the corridor on a permanent basis.


29 See Tex. Util. Code Ann. § 37.056(c)(4)(A – E).

30 See Oncor & LCRA – TSC Ex. No. 5 at 45 (Routes 295 & 296); and Cherokee Creek Ptnrs. Ex. No. 20 at 4.

31 See Newman Group Ex. No. 2 at 0024:18 – 0026:2.

                                       Newman Group’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief


          17.      Significantly, the diagonal orientation of Link J6 through Cherokee Camp means

the transmission corridor would not follow any property boundary or natural feature that would

minimize its intrusion on ranch operations.32 It would cut across the ranch interior, bisecting

pastures and habitat areas in a manner that maximizes disruption to the property’s functional

integrity. This is in contrast to routes – including Route 894 – that navigate the same general

corridor without imposing this impact.

          18.      The passage of Link J6 through Soldier’s Hole warrants separate attention.

Newman’s testimony documents the historical significance of this site to the property and the

broader cultural landscape of San Saba County.33 PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(C) requires the

Commission to consider “historical and aesthetic values” as a factor in route selection.34 A 765-kV

transmission line corridor passes through a historically significant site permanently and irrevocably.

Once the ROW is cleared and the structures are erected, the visual and physical integrity of the

site is permanently altered. The Commission should give meaningful weight to this impact when

comparing Route 894 – which avoids Soldier’s Hole entirely – to Routes 295, 296, and CCG that

do not.

                   2.       Route 894 Avoids Link K41 and NSP’s Dwelling on Tract 1447

          19.      Route 572 uses Link K41.35 The record establishes that NSP’s dwelling on Tract

1447 lies within approximately 450 feet of the Link K41 centerline – inside the Commission’s 500-

foot prudent avoidance zone.36 This is not a marginal case. A structure at 450 feet from the

35 See Oncor & LCRA Ex. No. 5 at 46 (Route 572).

centerline of a 765-kV line is not on the boundary of the prudent avoidance zone; it is well within

it. And as the testimony at the hearing confirms, the relevant zone of electromagnetic influence for

a 765-kV facility may extend beyond the conventional 500-foot prudent-avoidance metric,

meaning the 500-foot threshold may itself understate the prudent avoidance concern for a 765-kV

facility.37

          20.        The Commission’s prudent avoidance obligation requires that, where the

Commission is choosing among a set of viable routes, it should select the route that minimizes

residential exposure. As stated above, Route 572 would place a 765-kV transmission line 450 feet

from an occupied home on Tract 1447. Route 894 avoids Link K41 entirely.38 No routing

justification can support selecting Route 572 – with its compounded disadvantages across structure

counts, length, cost, and the K41 prudent avoidance concern – over Route 894, which avoids all

of those harms.

          C.         Route 894 Has No Adverse Parks Proximity Impacts – PURA Section
                     37.056(c)(4)(A)

          21.        Route 894 crosses zero parks or recreational areas and has zero feet of right-of-way

within the foreground visual zone of any park or recreational area.39 Among all 122 routes filed in

this proceeding, the range of ROW within the foreground visual zone of a park or recreational

area is zero to 8.68 miles.40 Route 894 achieves the best possible outcome on both of these parks

proximity metrics. There is no other filed route that simultaneously achieves the combination of

near-minimum habitable structure impacts and zero parks foreground visual zone ROW that

Route 894 delivers.

          22.          The importance of this criterion is well-established in the record. The Project

corridor passes by or near two significant state parks: Post Oak Ridge State Park and Colorado

Bend State Park. Testimony at the hearing confirmed that the Texas Parks and Wildlife

Department (TPWD) had recommended a setback of up to five miles from the southern boundary

of Post Oak Ridge State Park.41 With respect to Colorado Bend State Park, Dr. Andrew Sansom

confirmed that construction immediately adjacent to Colorado Bend would have a significant

detrimental effect on the quality of the park experience.42

          23.          Former PUC Commissioner Will McAdams confirmed that TPWD did not

intervene and sent no recommendation letters to the Commission.43 When asked how the

Commission should evaluate TPWD’s pre-application recommendations under those

circumstances, McAdams was unequivocal: “It’s not in the evidentiary record, so there’s nothing

to evaluate.”44

          24.          The absence of TPWD from the evidentiary record does not diminish the

significance of parks proximity as a routing criterion; it simply means that the Commission must

weigh that criterion based on the objective routing data in the record. On that data, Route 894 is

unambiguously superior: zero foreground visual zone impacts versus as much as 8.68 miles on the

worst-performing routes. Selecting Route 894 ensures that the Project is sited consistently with the

Commission’s obligation under PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(B) to protect recreational and park

areas and with the natural heritage values that those parks represent.

          D.        Route 894 Is Cost-Effective

          25.       The estimated transmission line cost for Route 894 is $1.681 billion.45 Route 894 is

less expensive than every route the Newman Group opposes:

                •   Route 295 at $1.683 billion ($1,975,000 more than Route 894);

                •   Route 296 at $1.685 billion ($3,644,000 more);

                •   Route 572 at $1.689 billion ($8,330,000 more); and

                •   CCG at $1.755 billion ($73,687,644 more).46

Stated differently, adopting Route 894 rather than Route 572 or CCG – the two most expensive

of the four alternatives the Newman Group opposes – would save ratepayers between $8.3 million

to $73.7 million in estimated transmission line construction costs, while also delivering superior

outcomes on habitable structure impacts, parks proximity, and landowner impacts.

          26.       Route 894 is also shorter than Route 572 and CCG. Route 894 is 223.2 miles in

length.47 Route 572 is 225.7 miles in length.48 And CCG is over nine miles longer at 232.2 miles.49

The shorter route reduces both construction costs and long-term maintenance obligations. Among

the full set of routes, Route 894 is approximately 2.73 percent more expensive than the very least

costly of all 122 filed routes, and approximately 9.52 percent less expensive than the costliest.50

Route 894 thus occupies a highly competitive position in the cost distribution while delivering the

full range of community, environmental, and landowner protections described in this brief.

         27.      Importantly, the Commission’s cost analysis should be conducted on an apples-to-

apples basis – comparing Route 894’s cost not in isolation, but relative to the routes with which it

competes. On that comparison, Route 894 is cheaper than Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG; it is

shorter than Route 572 and CCG; and it is superior on every non-cost criterion relevant to the

Newman Group’s interests. The cost record provides no basis for preferring any competing route

over Route 894.

V.       THE NEWMAN GROUP OPPOSES ROUTES 295, 296, 572, AND CCG

         28.      Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG each fail to meet the applicable routing criteria

under PURA Section 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC Section 25.101(b)(3)(B) in ways that each provide

compelling, independent grounds for rejection. The following sections address each route in turn.

         A.       Reject Routes 295 and 296

         29.      Routes 295 and 296 are inferior to Route 894 on four independently dispositive

grounds: (1) they use Link F34, which passes within 500 feet of the brand-new Florence ISD

elementary school serving approximately 500 students daily; (2) they use Link J6, which bisects

Cherokee Camp’s commercial hunting ranch and passes through Soldier’s Hole; (3) they expose

more habitable structures to the line than Route 894; and (4) they cost more than Route 894. Each

of these grounds independently supports rejection. Together, they compel it.

         30.      First: Florence ISD Elementary School and Link F34 – Prudent Avoidance. Both

Routes 295 and 296 use Link F34.51 A brand-new Florence ISD elementary school, serving

approximately 500 students daily, is counted among the habitable structures within 500 feet of the


51 See id. at 45 (Link F34 is in Routes 295 & 296).




                                                      Page 13 of 19
                                      Newman Group’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief


Link F34 centerline.52 This is not a marginal case. Five hundred children plus teachers and support

staff concentrated in a single building within 500 feet of a 765-kV transmission line is not a marginal

prudent avoidance concern – it presents a compelling reason to reject these routes. The

Commission’s prudent avoidance obligation applies with at least equal force to schools as to

residences. The concentration of 500 children in one location amplifies that concern beyond any

individual household.

         31.       The Save the Lampasas Group expert routing witness Brewer did not address the

Florence ISD school in his direct testimony.53 That omission is itself telling: a witness presenting

Link F34 as part of a viable route should have addressed a nearby school serving 500 children in

the prudent avoidance analysis. Route 894 does not use Link F34 and does not implicate this

concern.54 The Florence ISD new elementary school’s presence is an independent ground to reject

Routes 295 and 296 regardless of any other deficiency.

         32.       Second: Link J6 and Soldier’s Hole. Both Routes 295 and 296 use Link J6, which

bisects Cherokee Camp’s high-fenced commercial hunting ranch and passes directly through

Soldier’s Hole.55 As described above, the impacts of Link J6 on Cherokee Camp’s operations and

on the historical integrity of Soldier’s Hole are severe and irreversible. The Commission’s

obligation under PURA Section 37.056(c)(4)(C) to consider historical values is not satisfied by

noting that Soldier’s Hole lacks a THC marker; it requires the Commission to give weight to the

historical significance of documented sites on private land. Route 894 avoids Link J6 entirely and

therefore avoids this impact. Routes 295 and 296 do not.

             33.   Third: habitable structure counts. Routes 295 and 296 have 104 and 105 habitable

structures, respectively, within 500 feet of their centerlines, compared to 85 for Route 894.56 Under

the Commission’s prudent avoidance policy, this disparity compels the selection of Route 894 over

Routes 295 and 296 unless some other criterion provides a compelling countervailing justification.

The record contains no such justification.

             34.   Fourth: cost. Route 295 is estimated at $1.683 billion and Route 296 at $1.685

billion, compared to $1.681 billion for Route 894.57 Both routes cost more than Route 894. No

cost-based justification supports choosing either over Route 894.

             35.   In summary: Routes 295 and 296 use: (a) Link F34, which passes within 500 feet of

a Florence ISD elementary school serving 500 children daily; (b) Link J6, which bisects Cherokee

Camp and substantially impairs the historical integrity of Soldier’s Hole; (c) expose more habitable

structures to the line’s proximity than Route 894; and (d) cost more than Route 894. Each

deficiency independently provides a compelling reason to reject these routes. No combination of

advantages on any other criterion can outweigh these compounded failures when a superior

alternative – Route 894 – is available in the record.

             B.    Route 572 Must Be Rejected

             36.   Route 572 is more expensive, longer, and more impactful to residential

communities than Route 894 on every quantitative routing metric. Route 572 is more expensive:

$1.689 billion versus $1.681 billion for Route 894, a difference of $8.33 million.58 Route 572 is

longer: approximately 225.7 miles versus 223.2 miles for Route 894.59 Route 572 has substantially

more habitable structures: 107 within 500 feet versus 85 for Route 894 — a difference of 22

additional households exposed to the line’s proximity.60
